first.rationale: Competitor pricing pressure makes promotional_pricing tempting, but memory_73's 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' claim needs verification against the primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue—price-matching a competitor risks attracting low-LTV, price-driven accounts and could trigger a margin-eroding race to the bottom rather than durable revenue. Meanwhile, two concrete internal metrics are degrading right now (activation -6%, onboarding completion -4%), and memory_31 and memory_86 both point to onboarding/signup simplification as a lever that improved exactly these metrics durably and organically, without competitive-reaction risk. I verify memory_73 to confirm whether its 'strong lift' held up long-term or was short-lived/margin-negative, and memory_86 to confirm the onboarding-completion effect size is real and durable before committing this week's single experiment slot to it. Given only one slot, I favor the safer, directly metric-aligned lever (onboarding simplification) over a reactive pricing move, running it as a small guarded test rather than a broad rollout to preserve optionality and avoid over-committing based on inherited claims alone.

final.rationale: Verification confirms the decision. exp_73 shows targeted discounting produced strong short-term acquisition and revenue but a -12% 30-day retention hit, with the source explicitly warning not to generalize discounting as sustainable growth—this directly disqualifies promotional_pricing despite competitive pressure, since it would sacrifice the primary objective (sustainable long-term qualified revenue) for a cohort that churns before renewal. exp_86 confirms shortened onboarding improves completion (+13%), time-to-value, and even retention (+3%), corroborating memory_31's related finding on signup simplification and directly addressing the current onboarding-completion decline (-4% QoQ) and likely contributing to the activation decline (-6% QoQ) as well. With only one experiment slot this week, simplify_onboarding is the best-verified, lowest-risk, metric-aligned choice: it targets two of the three live problems (activation and onboarding decay) with a confirmed durable and retention-positive effect, while avoiding the discounting trap that would erode long-term value. I keep scale at small_guarded_test rather than broad_rollout because although exp_86 is confirmed, this week's execution context (competitive pressure, multiple concurrent declines) still introduces some novel conditions not present in the original experiment, so I preserve uncertainty and avoid over-committing before observing this week's results.
